utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. IT-04-74-T, Prlic et al. versus the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ken Scott, Vassily Poryvaev, and our case manager Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now turning to the Defence counsel. For the record, can you please introduce yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Michael Karnavas, counsel for Jadranko Prlic, along with Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel, and Ana Vlahovic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Mr. Bruno Stojic is represented by myself, Senka Nozica, and our case manager Mr. Slonje Valent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For accused Mr. Slobodan Praljak, counsel Bozidar Kovacic, co-counsel Mrs. Pinter, Nika Pinter, and our case manager Valentina Ivic. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Vesna Alaburic, Defence counsel for Milivoj Petkovic. My case manager, Mr. Davor Lazic, is accompanying me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Tomislav Jonjic, appointed Defence counsel for Mr. Coric. Next to me is Krystyna Grinberg, legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Pusic, Roger Sahota, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and case manager Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Trial Chamber, let me greet everybody after this long weekend; the accused, the Defence counsel, and the Prosecution representatives, not to forget all the people who support our work today. We are going to start our hearing with a first witness, but before the witness is brought in, let me give you a few explanations in housekeeping matters. As you know, the Trial Chamber issued a ruling on guidelines for the conduct of the trial on the 18th of April, 2006. We had received on a CD-ROM a chart from the Prosecution that failed to meet the requirements of the order of the 30th of November 2005. The amended decision of 18th of April is a reminder of the previous order of the 30th of November, 2005, requesting the Prosecution to present a chart, an amended chart, by the 4th of September, 2006. In other words, the Prosecution will have had nearly a year to prepare the chart, the proofing chart. So I don't want to hear the Prosecution say on the 4th of September that they did not have time enough to prepare the chart. You've got another several months ahead of you to complete the chart, so that, faithful to the principle of equality of arms, the Defence and the Judges can have a document making it possible to crossmatch witnesses and exhibits with specific references to Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). I'm sure you will do this very well. What I say for the Prosecution will of course in due course apply to the Defence. They will be under the same obligation. Second housekeeping matter: As you know, in the next few days, on Tuesdays and Wednesdays we will have sitting hours until 4.00 in the afternoon. But I have been told that witnesses need to have a bite and that they need at least one hour to do so, to have lunch. Otherwise, the witness may feel weak during the hearing, and he needs to be able to restore himself, and he needs an hour to do so. So this is going to be our schedule for the two long days in the week: Starting at 9.00, we will work from 9.00 to 10.30. We'll have a 20-minute break until ten to eleven. We'll resume at ten to eleven until twenty past twelve. Then we are going to have a lunch break for the witness from twenty past twelve to 1.20. For the witness and all those who want to eat something, of course. We will start again at twenty past one until ten to three with a break until ten past three, and we shall work from then until twenty to five for the two long days. I also wanted to tell you that, together with the Registry, I looked into the matter of a large screen in this courtroom. It might be possible to have large screen connected directly to the court deputy, and if you want to see a video excerpt or a see a large document, it will be possible to see it on the large screen. But there was a technical matter to be settled. If the Defence or the Prosecution want to zoom in on the document, can they do so directly or does it have to go through the court deputy? Because you know that normally it will be the court deputy who will do all the processing of a document. Well, if you are interested in this, please meet with the court deputy, Mr. Frejabue, and he will demonstrate to you how the system works. I've seen it personally and I think it might be useful for our work. I am the Presiding Judge, and as such under the Statute it is my onus to make sure that the proceedings unfold smoothly. This is the reason why I looked into this matter. For a few minutes, I would like to deal with a topic in private session. It's not going to be long. Please, Mr. Court Deputy, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A witness is due to come in. He's going to be brought in. I'll have him to make the solemn declaration, after which he will be examined by the Prosecution. I hope that the Defence counsel have agreed among themselves for the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. I want to first make sure that you can hear what I say in your own language through the headphones. If it is so, say, "Yes, I can hear you, and I understand you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you, and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, madam. Before you make the solemn declaration, can you give me your name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Spomenka Drljevic. I was born on the 1st of July, 1954, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which town do you live today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reside in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to work at the Ministry of Defence, and I'm currently an official -- I'm currently a retiree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, madam. Please read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, madam. Please sit down. Before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, who is going to put questions to you, let me give you some information on the way your testimony is going to take place. You should be testifying today and part of tomorrow. You will first be examined by the Prosecutor, sitting on your right. Thereafter, the Defence counsel, who are on your left, through one or several of them, will cross-examine you and put questions to you. You have Judges in front of you. At any time, whenever they deem it appropriate, they can put questions to you if they feel the need to do so. If you should ever have a problem whatsoever, do not hesitate to let us know. I remind you that you made an oath to tell the whole truth and that, because of the solemn declaration, you're bound to tell the truth and not to tell lies, because a lie can be regarded as a crime to be prosecuted by this Tribunal. This is the general framework for your testimony. And I give the floor to the Prosecutor, I believe Mr. Mundis, since he's sitting in the front row and he has just had a cup of water, so he now can ask his questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Drljevic.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to start by asking you some questions and I'd like to draw your attention to the period 1990, 1991. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber in what town you were living in 1990, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: From birth I have lived in Mostar. I still live there. Also, in relation to the period you asked me about, I also lived in Mostar then. At the time I used to work as a representative of a company from the town of Ploce. I worked in that capacity until the 31st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 31st of December, 1991, with respect to your employment with this company.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: In late March, early April, 1992, I received a dismissal letter which was retroactive, and I had no right to appeal. They also offered me to work as an exclusive representative of this company. The company is called Kartonplast, from the town of Ploce. It wasn't until two years ago that I found out that there is an association, which I joined in Jelah. I learned that there was a decision of the Croatian government from that period of time stating that all of those who do not have a place of residence in the Republic of Croatia are to be fired. The members of this association that I was in contact with, and also in some TV programmes, I heard that there were about 100.000 mostly Bosniaks and Serbs in a similar situation; people who were fired during that period of time. This association that I joined currently has about 10.000 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, when you told us that you received in late March or early April, 1992, a dismissal letter, what was the -- what was the stated reason in that dismissal letter for you losing your job?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: They stated as a reason lack to fulfil my duties for a number of months. Or, rather, they said that there was a lower demand which -- sales demand, which lasted for a number of months. At the time, the situation was not a stable one, either in Croatia or in Bosnia, so I took it as something that was inevitable. At any rate, this is something that I will deal with in the future, together with lawyers from Zagreb and this company in view of the fact that there are a number of contradictory issues there. The decision on employment, at least according to the then laws of Yugoslavia, specified that there was a probation period which could exist only when one was just starting to work, which was not my case. There was no reason to fire me at the time when I worked for them, and I interpreted this dismissal as something that was caused by the existing situation in the then Yugoslavia, and especially in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you elaborate or be more specific when you say "the existing situation in the then Yugoslavia, and especially in Bosnia." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: What I have in mind is this period of time, mostly 1991, because the war was well underway in Croatia at the time. The town of Ploce was shelled. This is a port in Croatia where my company was headquartered. We had telephone contact with them. However, in late 1991, it was already somewhat dangerous to travel through Bosnia, especially to some areas. So that was the main reason. In addition to that, people refrained from signing contracts and entering new deals. So that was the reality that we lived in. There was little work. However, Croats were not dismissed and other people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following your dismissal from this company, Ms. Drljevic, can you tell us where you were next employed, and approximately when.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't get employment in Mostar. We could say that the war broke out already in September of 1991 when reservists came to town. I think that it was on the 19th of September. However, there were no specific clashes. More provocation, intolerance. Serb soldiers were passing through, a lot of people were getting drunk. And this lasted up until the 3rd of April, 1992, when a truck carrying fuel exploded in the northern camp, and this is when the war broke out in town. There was occasional firing during night, also shelling. Then that started happening during daytime as well. And in April of 1992, I took four children of my sister to my friends in Kastela. This is an area comprising five or six small settlements near Split. I stayed there for about 15, 20 days, until my sister arrived -- or, rather, she came to visit the children, and I used that opportunity to go back to Mostar. And this is where I saw a terrible sight; destruction, shelling. In addition to that, I also learned that her father had remained on the left bank. Later on, I heard that he was taken to a Chetnik camp in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, ma'am. When you say "the left bank," what exactly are you referring to and what is the significance of the left bank?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "the left bank," I have in mind the left bank of the Neretva River. Before the war, it was mostly populated by Bosniak and Serb residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what about -- what about the right bank of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: The right bank of the Neretva River, yes, the western portion of the town, had more of a mixed population. I think that Croats were the dominant group in terms of numbers, although a lot of Bosniaks and Serbs also had apartments in Western Mostar, or, rather, on the right bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me take your attention, ma'am, to that period in April or May, 1992, when you returned to Mostar. After your return, did you gain any form of employment?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was absurd to even think of looking for new employment. I started searching for my father, and I found some young man who lived in the part of the town where I was born. It was the street called Husinjske Bune. And thus I decided to join this unit. At the time it was still a company, not yet a battalion. And those were mostly young men from this area and then from another building in Jankovci. At the time, I learned that several days before the 1st of May the Party of Democratic Action, which at the time was a leading Bosniak political party, had signed an agreement with the Croatian Democratic Union about the HVO being an armed formation which was going to defend Mostar. However, at the same time an Independent Mostar Battalion was also established. I don't know whether that was May or June, 1992. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, when you mentioned the Independent Mostar Battalion, was that in fact the unit of the army that you joined?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, where that unit, the Mostar Independent Battalion, was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: The Independent Mostar Battalion was located in various sites, depending on which company. I think that in May and June -- yes, May and June, there existed a Joint Command in the Vranica building. It was in Stjepan Radica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, when you say May and June, can you tell us what year that was, please.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: 1992. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again when you indicate to us, ma'am, that it was a Joint Command, can you tell us what were the components of this Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say. I can't answer that. I know that the battalion was composed of companies, and the first commander of the battalion was Suad Cupina. Later on, it was Semso Hasic, and for a time Arif Pasalic until the brigade was formed in July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago the HVO being an armed formation which was going to defend Mostar. Was the unit that you joined, that is the unit that you were a member of, was that part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I think it was, in view of the fact that on the letterhead you had both the chequerboard and the lily signs, emblems. But to tell you the truth, this wasn't something that I focused on at the time. What was important for me was that I was there to help the unit out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Drljevic, what was your specific role within the unit?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically from the very beginning, I was mostly there to be there. To clean up, to make coffee, to make some sandwiches in view of the fact that in May, 1992, the young guys moved to Goranci, which is a hill above Mostar. And I would go there every day, report for duty. I would make lists of those who volunteered, until the 3rd or 6th of June when a shell fell and hit the window of Lesnina. There was nobody in the basement, so there were no casualties, just some damage at the entrance across the way. We would see this in other locations because the unit that I belonged to or, rather, the company that I belonged to did not have a set place allocated to it until a little before they moved to the left bank, which means about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, ma'am, when you say "they moved to the left bank," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I meant my own unit, first of all. Members of the Luka Company in the Independent Battalion. But the crossing of the Neretva River was organised, and the members of the Independent Battalion took part in it and organised it, as well as the Croatian Defence Council, and it was crossing the Neretva River during the night, and they had to force various positions. From Rastani and the position of the Marsala bridge, or Tito's bridge, and further to the south near the Hasan Brkic bridge, in fact, and that took place between the 14th and 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did your company move to on the left bank? What location did you actually move to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, during those first few days, I did not go there. I arrived there around the 20th of June. First of all, we were put up in a private house which was a bakery, served as a bakery as well, in Marsal Tito Street, halfway between Lucki bridge and Saric mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Moving on, Ms. Drljevic, to July, 1992: Where was your unit at that point in time headquartered?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my unit already in July -- the 1st Mostar Brigade was established, and its headquarters were in Vranica. As to my battalion, together with some additional units attached to the staff, it was in the South Camp barracks. The battalion commander was Midhat Hujdur. He was appointed. When I reported to the unit for the first time he was the deputy of Enver Salcin who was the first commander of the Luka Company. During June, while they were advancing, while the units of the Luka Company, Donja Mahala, and so on, as they were advancing towards the Chetniks or, rather, the Chetniks were fleeing in part, leaving behind artillery weapons, artillery pieces, which were brought down to the streets and then collected up on the right bank of the Neretva River, or in North Camp, which is where the OH -- O -- HVO was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, Ms. Drljevic, that is the summer of 1992, your unit, which was a part of the 1st Mostar Brigade, and the HVO were engaged in fighting against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But already on the 9th of July, when there was large-scale shelling, and I think that there were aeroplanes as well that were firing, that the HVO units withdrew. I did not take part in that, I just heard about it from my commanders. This was also happening along the Chetnik lines further in-depth towards Cobanovo Polje, so that when we would take up our shifts a part of the territory would have been lost. But I don't think that I am the right person and competent enough to speak about this strictly military aspect. I'm sure you have better witnesses at your disposal who will be better able to tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, can you tell the Trial Chamber in general terms the ethnic composition of the 1st Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, the 1st Mostar Brigade was multi-ethnic, but mostly it was made up of the Bosniaks. Then you had a certain number of Serbs who stayed on in town and didn't leave with the Chetniks, and there were also some Croats who - how shall I put it? - found themselves in those districts and were -- and joined the units that were there. When I speak about and refer to Mahala, I mean the old parts of town, the old districts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about any changes in the structure of your brigade towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question. What were you referring to? At the end of 1992 there were a number of brigades that were established and formed a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm referring to, ma'am. Can you tell us a little bit about the establishment of the corps in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the policy coming from Sarajevo, and also the number of people who joined up with the units increased, in view of the fact that in 1992, exclusively under the command of the HVO, you had a unit of the Ministry of Defence that was active. So that people who were included in the army units were not included through the Defence Ministry but were included and joined up on an exclusively voluntary basis. As the number of units increased, there were many people who came in, who were expelled from Nevesinje, and they set up the Nevesinje Battalion. Then from Gacko as well. There were many people who arrived from there and from Bileca camp. They arrived in August, 1992. When the Gacko Battalion was set up - it was called Sargan - I can't tell you the exact figures, the numbers, but a certain number of people from Stolac as well who did not want to join the HVO in Stolac came to South Camp and set up the Bregava Brigade. I think that was in August or September, 1992. And then there was the Independent Battalion of Dreznica, a company in Blagaj, a brigade in Jablanica, and then there was the battalion in Buturovic Polje and the brigade in Konjic. So that an order arrived, I think on the 15th or the 17th of November, 1992, about the formation of the 4th Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina, and that was to be led by the man who was appointed, the late Arif Pasalic. And the commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade was - and he's also dead now - Midhad Hujdur, Hujka. I don't think I need give you the names of the other commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, then, Ms. Drljevic, what you're telling us is that by the middle of November, 1992, a corps, the 4th Corps, of the ABiH was formed in Mostar that included all of these brigades and units that you've just mentioned. Would that be a fair summary of what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What -- at the time the 4th Corps was established in mid-November, 1992, what was the relationship between the 4th Corps and HVO units in and around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was quite proper. I can say that. Well, I omitted to state beforehand that in the units of the Croatian Defence Council there were also many Bosniaks organised within it since the HVO had far more weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: But I think that already at that time there were misunderstandings over weapons. Contingents -- a contingent was supposed to reach the 4th Corps. But I have to say that I learnt about this only indirectly, quite by chance. I happened to hear about it quite by chance. So I would ask a question here or there. And I don't know whether it was September or exactly what month it was, perhaps October, when a truck was supposed to arrive in Mostar with weapons, but it didn't. And I know that there was some negotiations in Goranci and I think that was the only time -- the only truck that passed through to South Camp in Vranica. Well, I don't really know. I don't know what channels weapons arrived through. There were people who were in charge of that kind of thing. It was their wartime assignment and their duties, and that was the description of their job. That was the kind of work they did. So at one point in time there was some mention of the fact that a certain commander in Bijelo Polje, Andric, Car Andric, had stopped a large convoy. And Mira Cupina was in charge of that convoy. And it was a sum of 800.000 German marks was rumoured, was bandied about, but I don't really know. I didn't see any documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, ma'am, if you can tell us about the evolving nature of the relationship between the 4th Corps of the ABiH and the HVO at the end of 1992 into the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, there was a characteristic situation -- well, can I go back a bit in time, please, back to 1992? In October, 1992, it was rumoured that HVO units had attacked Prozor, and during that period Hujdur and Pasalic -- I'll refer to them by their full names. Pasalic, that's the surname of the corps commander. That they went to Prozor to see what the situation was like down there. But I think that they kept it rather a secret. We didn't know what it was all about. During that period, a number of volunteers reported, and they were led by Suad Muharemovic, who is a colonel now. They wanted to go and reinforce the troops liberating Jajce. However, they were sent back from some villages around Vakuf. And the explanation given was that the HVO and the army was already at war there, fighting there. In November, 1992, in an operation called Bura, the HVO took part only with artillery weapons from Hum hill, while the army units, BH army units, unfortunately, unsuccessfully attempted to attack Podvelezje. In December, 1992, the army units went to Mount Igman as reinforcements, but they did not -- members of the HVO did not take part in that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, ma'am, let me interrupt you there. When you talk about this operation called Brua, or Bura, in November, 1992, you said the HVO took part only with artillery weapons from Hum. Against what force was that operation directed?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That was an operation against the Chetnik forces which were located in Podvelezje, the relay station there, and throughout Podvelezje, that is to say the hill behind Mostar, on the mountain behind Mostar, to the east or, rather, on the left bank of the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me again ask if you could describe for us the relationship between the 4th Corps of the ABiH and the HVO in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Already, before, you could feel sporadic tension. And truth to tell, I personally can't say that I felt it myself; I heard about it from others. But in January, 1993, specifically, when the HVO issued an order according to which all the units should be resubordinated, that all units of the BH army should be resubordinated to HVO units and that the HVO was the sole legitimate authority in the area, especially in the Mostar region, then my commanders started to express their dissatisfaction, and I think that they expressed the will of most of the people who were in the unit. But at any rate, they were better versed in politics and the negotiations taking place with -- between the HDZ and SDA. And later on, there was a division in that party over that resubordination. In January, I was still in South Camp, and forms came to be filled in by the ITMS [as interpreted] people for material and technical equipment, forms relating to material and technical equipment. And there was an outcry against this. And there was an order whereby two remaining satellite antennae within the telecom factory, pursuant to an order by the corps commander, Pasalic, were handed over to the HVO. I think that later on these were used for the communications centre or the PTT links and communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record -- sorry to interrupt, ma'am, but for the record, can you tell us what ITMS refers to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's not ITMS. It's without the I. MTS; material technical resources. MTS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, that is January of 1993, what military force or forces controlled access to the city of Mostar in terms of the roads and other routes leading in and out of the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards Western Herzegovina and Croatia, all the approach roads and exits were controlled by the HVO. Even the civilians who were leaving town had to have HVO permits in order to be able to do so, exit permits. Up until a certain point in time, I can't tell you what exactly, and for all members leaving town, they could put in a request from the army. You couldn't leave town without an HVO permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about -- what about the roads to the north, the road from Mostar to Jablanica? In January, 1993, who controlled access along that road?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that road to Jablanica as also controlled by the HVO battalion from Bijelo Polje. That was the northern part, above Mostar to the north. Also to the south, towards Buna, it was also controlled by the HVO. For the requirements -- or, rather, for moving round town -- or, rather, you could move around town if you had permits allowing you to do so during curfew hours. The army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But as of January, 1993, those permits issued by the army were no longer in force. The police patrols didn't recognise them. Because I have to explain that there were people who had duties to attend to during the night. They had to tour the units, for example, or perhaps something else. In January, 1993, all exit and entrance points into Mostar were controlled by the HVO, and there were confiscations of certain quantities of goods being carried, or trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- Ms. Drljevic, can you explain what you mean by "confiscations of certain quantities of goods" carried by trucks? What type of confiscations? What type of goods? Who was doing the confiscating?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is only hearsay, but in the South Camp barracks, they had accommodation for the troops, but unfortunately, civilians would turn up there at the time too. And there was a truck driver who was there on one occasion, and that Buna in Ortijes - Buna is a place south of Mostar, and Ortijes is the location of an airport - but there is an air bridge in the vicinity, and the trucks used this bridge to go to the Suka factory [phoen] complex on the right bank of the Neretva River and to the south of Mostar. These were people from Bosnia who would spend a night or two there, and then sometimes people from the command would intervene, but on the whole we would send them to the HVO headquarters. We did this ourselves, because the HVO represented both the civilian and military authorities at the time. It was not possible to distinguish between certain fields of competence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Ms. Drljevic, about the presence of HVO military forces within the city of Mostar in the period April, early May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this order issued in January, 1993, the Bosniak side didn't accept the proposals. A deadline had been set, which was the 15th of April. By that time, the order was supposed to be executed. I think that during that period of time there was fighting in Jablanica. I know that the commander of the corps and Budakovic, his deputy, went to -- went to Jablanica in April. On the 16th and the 17th of April an attack was launched or there was an attempted attack on the Mostar Hotel, which is where the 4th Company and the command of the 2nd Battalion were located. There was an attack on Vranica, which is where the brigade command was located as well. On that occasion, two young men were wounded. They were guards. Their names were Crno Merovic and Kljako. Crnomerovic. Crnomerovic. It's one name; Crnomerovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The court reporters, ma'am, will --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see, ma'am, in the city of Mostar, large concentrations of HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, during that period of time. I couldn't provide you with the exact date, though, but at that time I had already moved to the Vranica command, and there were a lot of people. I couldn't say how many exactly. On one occasion I saw them in camouflage uniforms, and they were heading from the direction below Siroki Brijeg, which is where the stadium in Mostar is located, towards -- they were heading from that direction. And then they took the avenue to the old Velez pitch, and then they went towards Rondo. I don't know where they went then. I also saw a large number of people, a large number of men in black uniforms. I saw them in front of the Ero Hotel. My niece first mentioned the fact, and then one day I myself heard them speaking with a Dalmatian accent. We thought that they were just trying to mount a display of force, because the 15th of April was the army's day. And after review in front of the brigade command, troops marched down the avenue, which is near the mine. So the civilians from that area would approach us. They congratulated us. They felt that their morale had been given a boost. At that time, many members of the army were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just try to clarify what you've told us, if that's possible. These people -- you said a large number of men in black uniforms. Were these people in black uniforms members of the ABiH or the HVO or some other armed force?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that these men didn't have any insignia on them on that day when I saw that very large column. They had no insignia on them, but they certainly were not from Mostar. I don't know where they came from, where they had been brought in from. I don't know where they had been billeted. For some I assume they had been provided with accommodation in the Ero Hotel, but I don't think there was sufficient accommodation in town for all of them, so I'd say that they had found accommodation somewhere else. I couldn't really say they were from Croatia. This group, the group that I heard discussing some matters in front of the Ero Hotel, were from Dalmatia; they were Dalmatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This might be an appropriate point for our first break. I'm about to move into another subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Mundis. It is now half past three. We're going to have a break for 20 minutes, and we'll start again around ten to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, in just a moment I'm going to ask you about the events of 9 May, 1993, but before I do that I have one question from earlier this afternoon, and that relates to this: You've told us about units of the ABiH that were in Mostar and units of the HVO that were in Mostar. Other than those two armed forces, what other military forces, if any, were present in the city of Mostar in late 1992 or early 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. If I may object, I believe this question as it was put is a leading question. First, there should be a question whether there was any other beside those two forces, and then what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue, please, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, other than the HVO and the ABiH, were there any other military forces in the town or city of Mostar in late 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were Croatian army forces present there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there any other international military forces in the town of Mostar in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993, although I don't know what they were called at the time, but there were international military organisations in town at the time, but I don't know whether it was UNPROFOR. As for the period preceding the 1st of May, there was a transport unit that had something to do with the Projektant facility, and throughout that period of time it was patrolling throughout that area. It was perhaps a personnel carrier. It was in front of the Projektant facility during that period of time or, rather, it was at the crossroads where the Stjepan Radic Avenue is located. And it was in the direction of the new Velez stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, when you talk about international military organisations in town, do you know what country or countries this international military organisation was from?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say, but I know that this personnel carrier was a SpaBat personnel carrier. It was a Spanish UNPROFOR unit. But I wouldn't be able to tell you what it was called at the time. That's what the contingent was called; UNPROFOR, AROFOR [phoen], SFOR. The names change so frequently that I couldn't really say for sure what the precise name of that international military organisation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "SpaBat," can you tell us what "SpaBat" refers to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, I'd like to draw your attention now to the events of 9 May, 1993. Can you tell us where you were on the day immediately before 9 May; that is, on the 8th of May, 1993? Can you tell us where you were on that day?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, 1993, I was working in the command in Vranica. I was there until about 4.00 in the afternoon. I remember that it started to rain at that time, and at that time the president of the cantonal unit, Zijad Demirovic, and Emir Bijedic, I think he was part of the security for the 4th Corps, and then there was Demirovic and my commander, Hujdur, I know that they returned from a joint meeting. I think it was a meeting that had been held with the HDZ. And from the 17th or 19th of April, up until that day, a number of arrests of army members had been made. A number of arrests of ABiH members had been made. So -- had been made. So they were discussing things to see if they could find a solution to misunderstandings. A day prior to that meeting, two couriers had been arrested. Orhan Zilic was one of them, and the other was the son of Professor Semso Badzak. I don't know what his name is. They were released that very same day. A few days earlier, a group of about 15 soldiers had also been arrested. They were returning from the lines in Podvelezje. And when you take all these factors together, they contributed to creating a very tense atmosphere. I asked them whether I should stay on, whether they needed assistance of any kind. The commander said I should sleep over somewhere in the building, because I lived on my own in my flat. And on that day -- on that day I was in uniform, and he said that anyone who was in army uniform would be arrested. He said that was being done. And a little earlier I had told him a joke of some kind. I had some -- a change of clothes in my bag, toothpaste and toothbrush. I had that with me in case they would not recognise the permit I had been issued with in order to be able to move around freely during the curfew. I thought this would only last for a day or two. So I decided to stay in the building. Up until 8.00, I was near the entrance facing the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the police station. I was with my friend Dzenana. But as there was nowhere for me to sleep, I went to the Vranica building. There was a married couple there, Svjetlana and Edo Turajlic. And I think they were on the fourth or fifth flat, or they lived on the fourth or fifth flat in that building. On the fourth or fifth floor in that building. I recently watched the film Escape from Alcatraz on television, but at any case, at 5.00 in the morning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: At the time they were watching that film, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was woken up by shots, and then I saw that a shell had hit that flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, when you make reference to 5.00 in the morning, can you tell us what day you're now talking about?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 9th of May. As I've already said, on the 8th of May in the evening or, rather, after 4.00 p.m., I stayed on to sleep at my friend's place. I am talking about the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, what year is that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, was the ABiH command, the personnel of the ABiH command in the Vranica building or were they somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th or 19th of April, we had additional guards. There were 20 or 30 young men providing security for the building. Up until that time, there had only been four or five of them. It wasn't necessary to have more of them. And this is what was changed when these two young men were wounded. There were no commanders there. I don't think it was necessary. I assume that the commander Hujdur wasn't familiar with the situation. I'll say something more about this later on. He turned up on the 8th at about 9.00 in the evening. He visited those on duty. I wasn't present, but that's what I was told in the morning. His aunt stayed on in the building. She had brought him up and I'm sure he wouldn't have left her there had he known that there'd be an attack, had he known that there would be such a destructive attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, let me return to the events of the early morning of 9 May, 1993. You've told us that at 5.00 in the morning you were woken up by shots and you saw that a shell had hit the flat. Where did you go after waking up?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I got dressed and I went down, because the brigade command was in the cellar of the building. I'll have to explain this. Vranica is the name for that complex of buildings. It's the name of this construction company there, and part of the management was located beneath that building, and its archives were located there too. The corps command was in Vranica and it was in the entrance where the construction company was located before the war, and during the war too. And in the part in front of the Stjepan Radica Street where a leather and textile company was located, well, in that part there was some sort of a shop from Visoko - it didn't function during the war - and that's where the unit was located, the unit from the 1st Mostar Brigade -- or, rather, the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade. I apologise. On that evening, the usual officers were on duty, the communications officer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you arrived, ma'am, in the Vranica -- in the basement of the Vranica building on 9 May, 1993, how many members or how many soldiers of your unit were present there?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: When I went to the cellar, there were about 10 individuals there. I saw them immediately. The young men from the communications centre, there was the chief of the communications centre, there was the duty officer, an operations officer, Jusuf Rodovic. And at the entrance to the building or, rather, in the cellar, since that's where the command was located, there was a wounded man who was about 60 years old, Enver Zekic. He had been wounded in the stomach. He had either been shot or hit by a piece of shrapnel, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution -- or the document that's been marked as 9413, which is actually a photograph. If we could please -- if we could please go to the pages marked with ERN number 02068382. I believe that's page 4 of this document or photo book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you please tell us what you see on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I can see the buildings that go by the name of Vranica in the first photograph. It's not really visible here, but since I passed by that building on two occasions about three years ago and also a couple of months ago, I know that -- in the first photograph you can see the entrance that was used by the corps command. They entered the building through that entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, Ms. Drljevic, "that entrance," can you please describe for us where in the photograph -- or perhaps if the touch pen is working, we can ask the witness to ...

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: You can only see one entrance here. You can see the bars over the window. This is the window. And here it says Vranica. You have a sign that says Vranica. And this is the entrance that members of the corps command used, as well as the young men who provided security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, ma'am, is that the entrance that members of your unit used in entering the building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That's the entrance used by members from my command. It's the entrance for the 4th Corps, and the entrance to the corps command was somewhere else. Could we have a look at the other photograph? There are some trees here, and this is where the entrance to the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, the witness is how referring to the photograph with the ERN number 02068383. In the bottom centre of that photograph there is a kiosk. Immediately adjacent to the kiosk is the tree to which the witness was referring where she indicated that that was the entrance to the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what happened after you arrived in the cellar of the Vranica building on the -- or in the early morning hours of 9 May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the cellar, in addition to the ten soldiers I saw at the time - some of them I've only seen in video recordings, in photographs - but there was some women and children from the building who were there too. Apart from the local inhabitants, there were many refugees from the left bank whose houses had been burnt in the fights with the Chetniks. They had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, how long did you remain in the basement of the Vranica building after you arrived there in the early morning hours of 9 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained there up until the afternoon of the 10th May. Some of the young men who had been allocated to various floors and to the corps, I saw them during those two days and nights. Some women prepared, as much as they could under the intensive shelling and fire, some food. They would go upstairs, bake bread, and then come back to the basement. The attack did not come as a surprise -- the attack was a surprise to us, therefore we did not have previously prepared food. The firing was very intense. These houses remained in this condition for at least ten years after that, and you can see the type of calibre that was used. That whole time, we had contact with the forward command post of the brigade of the corps on the left bank, which was in the SDK building. They asked from the communications centre to ensure that Dr. Selma Jakupovic and another male doctor would come. They were anaesthesiologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, if I could interrupt you at this point in time. In addition to the soldiers who were in the basement, you've told us about some women and children from the building. Approximately how many people in total were in the cellar of the building? And then if you could give us a breakdown as to how many were military and how many were civilian.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the accurate number, because some of the soldiers were on various floors while some were in the part where the corps members entered. And then again, some soldiers were in the entrance or, rather, in the building where the entrance is from Stjepan Radica Street where the Kluz shop was, and this is where logistics people were and people securing that area. As for soldiers, I can say that there were 30 to 40 of them, including the 13 listed as missing. As for civilians, I wouldn't want to speculate. Perhaps there were about 100 of them in these two entrances. When I say "two entrances," I mean all of the people who were there and assembled in front of the MUP building. But in that other area, maybe some 50 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us, ma'am, if I understood you correctly, that from the early morning of the 9th of May until the afternoon of the 10th of May, 1993, you were in the cellar of the Vranica building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber how it is that you came out of the basement of the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, I'd like to say that we had telephone contact with somebody from the HVO. Mostly they asked for Rudi, Rudi Jozelic, who was a duty officer. They wanted him to surrender, which he refused. And then they would accuse us on the radio of keeping civilians imprisoned. Upon hearing that, we told those who wished so to leave the building. However, nobody responded to that. I can tell you that the population or, rather, tenants of that building were mixed. There were Croats, Bosniaks, and most likely Serbs. I think that most of the people were afraid that the cease-fire would not be complied with. All of them remained there to the end. I remember that when Zekic was wounded, we asked for a -- for an emergency ambulance car, and they said that they could only send a truck with petrol. At one point Goran Zekic, whose father had been wounded, called on the phone Jadran Topic. They were family friends. He asked him to help him. However, he refused because Goran was very angry. He stormed out, and he wanted to start shooting, and then some guys went and fetched him back. Since I was quite exhausted, I withdrew and retired into that office. I maybe slept there for an hour, and then I was awakened by a group of people. I saw that some of them were missing, about half of them were missing, and then there was a little girl who was eight to nine years old and who was wounded in her head. I have to say that people started panicking somewhat. We knew that the upper stories of the building were on fire. They even brought down on stretchers a man who was suffocating from smoke, who had smoke inhalation problems. I think his last name is Kajic. I remember his face, but I'm not sure about his last name. Also, some water pipes had burst, so the floor was flooded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, ma'am, can you tell us about the efforts that were undertaken to get out of the cellar of the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: They were running out of ammunition. It was clear that we would be unable to defend ourselves. I would rather not go into evaluation of the situation. I know that some people wrote books about it. I didn't read the books, but apparently one could establish the number of soldiers engaged on the opposite side in order to make a comparison. At one point in time, since Rudolf was there the entire time -- from the inception of the brigade, he was there, and another man who previously used to work in Vranica was there as well, and they knew that one of the walls, partition walls in my office, had been erected previously. So they took out a brick ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, did they begin taking down the walls in the basement, in the cellar, as a means to trying to get out of that location?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may object -- if I may object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Mundis and I commend him, he's done an excellent job so far, though there have been some times where he's posing a question that is rather leading or it assumes a fact that is not in evidence yet. I think it's so important, at this stage at least, to get as much of the information from the witness as opposed to Mr. Mundis imparting that information on us and then having the witness validate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sustained. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you said, "So they took out a brick." Can you tell us what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I was shaken, because -- yes. They were taking bricks out one by one with their hands. The young man helping him is not on the list of missing. Nothing is known about his fate. So I apologise. I recreated this image in my mind. So there were four or five officers there who decided to attempt to leave that entrance. Since the people knew that this wall was just a partition wall with just plain bricks, they assumed that it would be easier to break through that wall -- or, rather, to remove that wall. I wouldn't be able to tell you who said that people should change into civilian clothes. Most people did that. So did I. But since this is something I stated in my previous statements, due to stress, I started bleeding, which lasted until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once they removed the bricks and made an opening big enough for one person to pass through, then we saw a metal door. The man Alica Pobric started firing. He started firing from an automatic rifle at the door and then the door opened. In the room next to it -- this was also in the basement, in the corridor, and then the stairs take you up to another entrance where there were many civilians. In addition to this girl and the young man who worked in encryption, Muradif Habibi -- his name is Muradif Habibija. He was wounded. He had a wound on his back, and there was a large haematoma next to his spine. So in addition to others, I also helped carry him out. In this other building -- this was actually the entrance where I went on the previous day to visit my friend. Dr. Jerko was there. There were also some men from Luka; Nino Sefic, Hasif Nemic, Corda, Dr. Dzeko was there, and Zijad Demirovic, who took it upon himself to negotiate. Since right next to that building is the MUP building, there were soldiers there who had surrounded the building, so he took it upon himself to negotiate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, if I could interrupt you at this point. A few moments ago you said, "... due to stress, I started bleeding, which lasted until --" and at that point the interpreters were unable to hear the name of the location. Can you repeat that part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Until Ljubuski. When Dr. Dzeko came and he gave me a rest of 15 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. You were at the point, ma'am, where you told us about some negotiations, the commencement of negotiations. Can you elaborate upon those negotiations; who was doing the negotiating and what the subject matter of those negotiations were?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zijad Demirovic, who at the time was president of the cantonal board of the SDA. He was an architect by profession, and he recently died. He took a loudspeaker and started talking to the soldiers who had surrounded the building and were standing around the building. He told them that we were civilians and arranged for us to leave the building one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, ma'am, where did you go -- or did you in fact leave the building one by one?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, one by one. However, in the part of the building that we had left, prior to that some 10 to 15 young men remained there in uniforms and weapons to attempt to break through to the surgical department. I don't know whose decision it was for them to remain there and for others to move to another part. I know that Emir Bijedic remained back there with them. At the time, he was assistant commander for security within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Ms. Drljevic, when members of the group left the building, the Vranica building, one by one, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this building or, rather, next to it at the time there was a yellow fence. It was definitely yellow then. I think that it's blue now. So this was a fence, a metal fence with upright bars. I don't know how I managed to get over that fence while carrying a young child in my arms. A friend of mine had two children, girls, who were one and a half. She carried one of them, and I carried the other one. We went over the fence and went towards the MUP building. Now it is the building of the city MUP. I saw Rudolf and Thedja [phoen] carrying somebody in a blanket. I don't know whether it was Muradif or the girl that they were carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, as you went towards the city MUP building, did you see any people in the immediate vicinity of that building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, what do you mean "people"? Do you mean soldiers perhaps? Soldiers, yes. I saw a large number of uniformed soldiers with ribbons. I don't know what colour the ribbons were, ribbons on their sleeves. Some of them stood there and directed us to tell us in which direction we were to move. Some of them stopped the large number of people from going to the surgical department. No, they directed us towards the fence. We were to go over the metal fence. And then right there in front of the building, they separated men from women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these soldiers, these uniformed soldiers with ribbons, what armed force were these soldiers a member of, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say whether they were members of some of the brigades or perhaps of MUP of Herceg-Bosnia [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "there in front of the building, they separated men from women," which building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the building of MUP, the MUP building. Once we went over the fence, they directed us towards that building. This is the building which houses the city MUP nowadays. This is where we go to get personal IDs and so on. This is where they separated men from women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did the women go?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: The women were taken inside the building to a room which resembles an amphitheatre. I don't know how to explain that. It must have been some kind of a conference room, and there were benches there lined up so that they are one above the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, ma'am, let me interrupt you there, because you say the women were taken inside the building. And again, can you be more specific as to what building you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the MUP building. That's what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Ms. Drljevic, the approximate date and time that the women were taken into the city MUP building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 10th of May, at around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Drljevic, do you know or did you observe where the men who had been with you in the basement of the Vranica building were taken once they were separated from the women?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Some of them remained in the other part of the building, and some of them were taken towards the stone building, which is to the east of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the street name. I just can't recall it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Nowadays this is where the cantonal MUP is housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear, then, you told us that some of them -- some of the men remained in the other part of the building and some of them were taken towards the stone building. Now, when you say some of them remained in the other part of the building, which building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm once again referring to the building where women were. I can't be fully certain, because on the following day I saw some of them on the floor upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, because we have -- Ms. Drljevic, we have to maintain the written record here, the building where the women were located, what is the name of that building, or what is currently in that building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was the building of the MUP of Herceg-Bosnia [as interpreted]. It is also the MUP building nowadays. Since Mostar has a peculiar organisation, municipal organisation, it is known as the city MUP, not a municipal MUP. So it's in the building known nowadays as the city MUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in the building that's known nowadays as the city MUP building, the women were kept and some of the men were kept. Is that what you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm trying to say. But I'm also trying to say that initially they were not in the same premises. The women were in this amphitheatre, and with us there was this young man who in early 1993 lost his leg. His name is Gosto Adis. And then there were women and children. I don't know where they took the men. It wasn't until the next day, where most of the women either went home or to Heliodrom, that I saw some of the men upstairs in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long, Ms. Drljevic, did you remain in this city MUP building after you arrived there on the 10th of May, 1993, at approximately 1500 hours?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained there until the 13th of May, late in the evening. It was night-time, very dark, maybe midnight. I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many other people were detained with you in the Mostar city MUP building during the time that you were there from the 10th through the 13th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I can say: On the 10th, 11th, we stayed in that room for two nights. Then on the 12th, a number of women were placed in a bus, and my friend was among them, and they were taken to the Heliodrom. During the night of the 13th, I noticed that some women would come out from time to time and then go back. And when they left the second time, they wouldn't come back so I assumed that they were people who had left the building. I didn't know them myself except for Jesenka Rajkovic Kragulj. She was a Bosniak married to a Croat, Tihomir Kragulj, who was in uniform. He was wearing a police uniform when he met me, and his words were, "Your time is up, Secretary." Otherwise, a few days before the attack, with him and with Zeljko Budimir, I had a cup of coffee, and I thought that everything was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, I'd like to return your attention to the time when you first arrived in the city MUP building on or about the afternoon of the 10th of May, 1993. Can you tell us, please, what happened when you first arrived in the city MUP building.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what you saw when you entered that building and where you were taken in that building.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That first day we were taken to that hall where they probably held their meetings, where there was such a large number of women. We spent another day there, and then those women were taken off by bus. They said that Bojana, Selma, and Mirna - they were journalists who worked at the radio - and I myself, that we would stay for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the course of the time from the 10th through the 13th of May, 1993, while you were in the Mostar city MUP building, were you in fact at any point in time interrogated?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, we had to state our identities, and we were told that all those without ID documents should come up to the table and introduce themselves, and that's what I was talking about earlier on. As I knew that woman, she was brought up by Hujdur's aunt, when they asked her what relation Hujka was to her, she said that he wasn't any relation at all -- or she. It seemed to me as if -- well, I think she replaced his mother, and it was like a mother giving up her own child. That's what it appeared to be like to me. I had no dilemmas. I introduced myself straight away and said that I was a member of the army, and I think that that -- well, I didn't know anybody, hardly anyone there, and I think that that made the people there leave me alone and instigate proceedings. But I'm not quite clear about that whole episode to this day. I don't know the reasons I was held or why I was held for such a long time or under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, you told us earlier that you left the city MUP building late in the evening of 13 May, 1993. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I just go back for a moment to the 12th or 13th, just back a bit before I fast forward, to turn the tape back? Upstairs, on the floor above, where they questioned us one by one, I was questioned for a very brief time. I knew Marin Jurica. He had a marketing agency or a fashion agency or some such thing. And his brother worked there before, and he interrogated me first with respect to my participation in the war and my stay in Vranica. I can't actually say that he was brutal or violent in any way. It was quite a proper interview. But at one point Mr. Demirovic, who was in the hallway outside, and Nino Sefic, Hajdarevic - I can't remember his first name now - Hazim Memic, Almir Corojevic, at one point, well, there were some offices and a long corridor or a long hallway at the end of which there was a television set, and it was switched on. And Mr. Demirovic was -- almost started crying, because somewhere in the column he recognised his wife, in the column of civilians that was moving across Varda. Varda is a hill to the south of Mostar, above the Heliodrom. I also saw -- and this was a programme that was called Slikom na Sliku. The journalist was Dijana Culjak. I saw them come out one by one, those young men who provided the security. Later on, I also watched this footage, but I can't say exactly where it was filmed, whether it was in front of the Vranica building at a spot where there is a makeshift shed, prefabricated shed, which is, I think, where the tax office is today, or something like that, or perhaps it might have been in front of the headquarters of the HVO, in front of the Parkova [phoen] or Lesnina building. I can't say now for sure, but at any rate, at the end of this footage they showed the people and their names and surnames who obviously knew where those young men were located. And among other things, I hope that this testimony of mine will contribute to us learning where the bones are at least. The young men were shown as they were taking out the picture of Sefer Halilovic and the emblem which indicates the fact that they had been taken prisoner and that that was how it was staged, because there is very little likelihood that people would otherwise have stood before an execution squad, for example, in that way, or whatever you like to call the people standing in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Could we now go to the time period when you left the city MUP building, and if you could please tell the Trial Chamber where you went.

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That night, as I say, it was late. After midnight. 11.00 p.m. or midnight. I think that that programme Slikom na Sliku was shown very late. Well, I don't know if it was that day or not, but anyway, all the people were wearing uniforms, and he said that we should collect up our belongings and go, and we even hoped that we were going home. Then the four of us were put into a police car with bars on the windows - and that particular type of vehicle is referred to as a Black Maria - and they drove us to the Kameni or stone MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again if I --

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: And there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you briefly. When you say "the Kameni or stone MUP," what building are you referring to? What location or building are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the cantonal MUP, as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately, ma'am, how far is the cantonal MUP building from the Mostar city MUP building?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very close by. Perhaps some 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what happened after they drove you to the Kameni or stone MUP building on that evening, 13 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't take us into the building. They brought us before the building, in front of the building. And then they took us in. I couldn't see anybody because it was dark, but at one point I saw that a woman had her hands handcuffed behind her back. We set out in a column. There was a car in front of us with rotational lights, three Kombi vans with the bars on the windows, and three vehicles with rotation lights behind us. There were two armed young men sitting in the -- inside of the van, and they just said -- they asked us whether we knew where we were going, and we said no, we thought we were going to the Heliodrom, but he said, "No. You're going to Ljubuski." I had just heard about Ljubuski as being some sort of central prison before that, and on one occasion I went there -- well, not where we were put up, but I went in 1992 when the group from Bileca was released. Anyway, when we arrived up there, they took us into a building, ordered us to stand up against the wall with our arms raised and legs spread, and they searched us and asked us to give our identities, to give our names and surnames. At that point in time, I did not see who else was brought in, but I did recognise the voice of Rudolf Jozelic, and a blow when, after asking, "What are you?" He said, "I'm a Bosnian Catholic." Then I heard this blow. Vlado Fink was there as well. And there was Kamenko Bosnjak, who was a journalist on radio otherwise. And when asked the same question, he said, "I'm here by mistake, sir," and they released him the very next day. I didn't recognise anybody else or the voice of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ms. Drljevic, if I can just ask you a few questions about this. Do you recall approximately what time it was and the date that you arrived in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th during the night. I don't know what time. It might have been one or two hours after we had left Mostar. I can't be sure of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in the group that was with you that was transported from Mostar to Ljubuski during the night of 13 March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps 20. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the gender and ages of the people that were transported with you on that evening?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I can't, because -- well, I can say that I know there were five of us women in the room later on. However, throughout that time while the people in the black uniforms were there, they weren't the people that we saw later on there. They were others who came as an escort. And they asked us to look at the wall, keep our eyes to the wall. So I don't know who actually came to Ljubuski that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, ma'am, approximately how long you remained in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in Ljubuski until the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the building or buildings that you were kept in during this period from 13 May until 8 June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SPOMENKA DRLJEVIC
utterances.text: That first night when we were brought there, there were no beds in the rooms, and quite obviously they weren't expecting any women to turn up, so that we sat on the floor that whole night. There was a table. They brought in beds the next day, and we were all put up in one room. There was this large room in which they placed the beds. There weren't any bars on the windows. There was a smaller room, too, but as several days later they brought in the men to clear up the parquet flooring, they made a makeshift sort of dining area, dining-room. And there was another building which I learnt later was where the men slept who were not detainees, who weren't prisoners. They were free men who were truck drivers from Bosnia. Up on the upper storey there were the premises of the police. They took me up there for interrogation, but I don't really know how many offices there were there.
